name: Gajra hair flowers

lead: The gajra is a garland of flowers worn by women in South Asia, mainly in India, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and parts of Pakistan. It is wound around a bun or woven into a braid for festivals, weddings and everyday traditional dress, and it dresses up a hairstyle with colour and scent.
Jasmine (mogra) is the most common flower, with roses, marigolds, tuberose, crossandra and others used by region and occasion. Artificial gajras in silk, cotton or crochet are also sold.

paras: A gajra is usually threaded on string, coiled or pinned around a bun or braided in, and kept cool and misted so it does not wilt. It is paired with traditional clothing and jewellery for weddings, festivals and dance performances.
There are no studies on health effects. Fresh flowers wilt over a day, and anyone with pollen or floral allergies may react.

angle.text: A gajra is an accessory: it changes how a hairstyle looks by adding floral colour and volume to a bun or braid, and it is a standard part of bridal and festival styling.

lead: A gajra is a flower garland worn in the hair by women in South Asia, mainly India, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and parts of Pakistan [1]. It is worn at festivals, at weddings including pre-wedding events such as haldi, mehndi and sangeet, and with everyday traditional dress [1].

As a styling element, the gajra adds colour, fragrance and a finished, traditional look to a bun or braid, though it generally decorates the style rather than holding it in place [1]. Jasmine is the most common flower, with roses, crossandra and barleria also used [1].
Gajras are documented in encyclopedic and cultural descriptions; no published human studies have examined them.

paras: Wikipedia describes the gajra as a flower garland worn by women in India, with jasmine the most frequent choice and rose, crossandra and barleria also widely used [1]. Grokipedia describes a typical length of about 12 to 18 inches coiled around a bun, braid or updo, with marigold for bright festival colour and roses and tuberose popular at weddings; it also lists artificial versions in silk, plastic, cotton or crochet [2].

Wikipedia shows jasmine gajras on hair buns in Gupta-era Ajanta paintings and on an eleventh-century Green Tara figure, and notes Odissi dancers wear imitation gajras made of sholapith [1]. Grokipedia suggests floral hair adornment may date to the Indus Valley Civilization, that garlands appear in Vedic texts and the Ramayana, and that the gajra became a courtly ornament in the Mughal era; it gives symbolism of purity, femininity and marital blessing [2]. These points come from an AI-generated encyclopedia and are less firmly sourced.

Gajras are worn on the hair bun or braid and also on the wrist at festive events and weddings [1]. They feature in bridal ritual adornment, in festivals such as Diwali and Teej, in Eid celebrations in Pakistan and in Bharatanatyam dance [2]. Bollywood films, notably Devdas in 2002, are credited with popularising the look, which now also appears in fusion and boho styles and online retail [2].
